title: How Much Should You Save Every Month If You Want to Buy Rental Property in the U.S.
description: Calculating the 'Cash to Close' for investment real estate.
content:
Buying a rental property is different from buying a home to live in. Lenders view it as a riskier transaction. You can't use 3% down payment programs; you typically need 20-25% down plus 'Reserves' (cash in the bank to cover vacancies). This high barrier to entry stops many aspiring landlords. To buy a cash-flowing property in 3 years, you need a specialized savings plan that accounts for the higher capital requirements of real estate investing.

Key Takeaways

  • The 25% Rule: For a non-owner occupied Investment Property, lenders usually require 25% down to get the best interest rate. On a $400k property, that is $100k cash.
  • Closing Costs: Budget 3-4% for closing costs. Investment loans often have higher origination fees (points) to buy down the rate.
  • Reserves: Banks require you to show 6 months of mortgage payments in liquid cash after the down payment. You can't drain your account to zero.
  • House Hacking Exception: If you live in one unit of a multi-family (duplex/quadplex), you can use an FHA loan with 3.5% down. This drastically lowers the savings target.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Interest rates for investment properties are typically 0.50% - 1.00% higher than rates for primary residences. Saving a larger down payment helps lower the monthly payment to ensure the property 'Cash Flows' (Rent > Mortgage + Expenses).

The Investor's Savings Target

Target: $300,000 Single Family Rental.

The Upfront Cash Stack

  • Down Payment (25%): $75,000.
  • Closing Costs (4%): $12,000.
  • Immediate Repairs: $5,000 (Paint/Flooring).
  • Reserves (6 Months): $10,000.
  • Total Cash Needed: $102,000.

The Timeline

If you want to buy in 3 Years (36 months):
$102,000 / 36 = $2,833/month.

Reality Check: This is a heavy lift. This is why most investors start with 'House Hacking' (living in the property) to use lower down payment loans, or partner with others to split the capital requirement.

Where to Store the Capital

  1. Risk Appetite: Since the goal is huge ($100k), you might be tempted to invest in stocks to get there faster.
    - Conservative: HYSA/CDs. Guaranteed to get there, but slow.
    - Aggressive: 20% Stocks / 80% Bonds. Try to beat inflation.
  2. The 'Opportunity Fund': Label this account 'Real Estate'. When you see a deal, you need liquidity instantly. Do not lock this money in 5-year CDs. Use Money Market Funds.
  3. REIT Interim: While saving, consider putting 10% of the fund into a REIT ETF (VNQ). This tracks real estate prices. If housing booms while you save, your savings grow too. If housing crashes, your savings drop, but so does the cost of the house you want to buy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use my 401(k)?

You can take a loan ($50k max), but it is risky. If the rental sits vacant, you have to pay the mortgage AND the 401(k) loan payment. Cash is safer.

What is DSCR?

Debt Service Coverage Ratio loans allow you to qualify based on the property's rental income, not your personal income. They often require 20-25% down but make it easier to scale.

Is 20% down mandatory?

For conventional investment loans, usually yes (or 15% with PMI). There are 'Hard Money' loans with lower down payments, but rates are 10-12%. Avoid these as a beginner.
